hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-02.title: Size comparison
hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-02.body:
Suppose $n$ has $k+1$ digits, the first being $d\ge1$. Then $n\ge d\cdot10^k$, while the product of its digits is at most $d\cdot9^k$. If $n$ equals the product of its digits then $d\cdot10^k\le d\cdot9^k$, which forces $k=0$.

So $n$ has one digit, and every one-digit number equals the product of its digits. The largest is $9$.

**Answer: 9**

hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-05.title: Square the sum
hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-05.body:
Let the sides be $x,y$. Then $x+y=5$ and $x^2+y^2=15$. Squaring the first, $x^2+2xy+y^2=25$, so $2xy=10$ and the area is $xy=5$.

**Answer: 5**

hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-06.title: Column subtraction
hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-06.body:
Since $D<A$, the units column needs a borrow: $D+10-A=C$. In the tens column, $(C-1)-B$ is negative (as $C<B$), so we borrow again: $(C-1+10)-B=A$. In the hundreds column $B-1\ge C$ (because $B>C$), so no borrow is needed there: $(B-1)-C=D$. In the thousands column $A-D=B$.

So $C=D+10-A$, $A=C+9-B$, $D=B-1-C$, $B=A-D$. Substituting $B=A-D$ into $D=B-1-C$ gives $C=A-2D-1$; combining with $C=D+10-A$ gives $2A=3D+11$, so $D$ is odd. Then $D=1$ gives $A=7$, $C=4$, $B=6$; check $7>6>4>1$. (Other odd $D$ give $A=13$ for $D=5$, too large, and $D=3$ gives $A=10$, too large.)

Check: $7641-1467=6174=BDAC$. ✓.

**Answer: $(7,6,4,1)$**

hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-07.title: Similar triangles
hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-07.body:
Since $BD\parallel AE$, triangle $BCD$ is similar to triangle $ACE$, and the ratio of similarity equals $CX:CY=5:8$ (the line $CY$ meets the parallel lines $BD$, $AE$ at $X$, $Y$).

So $[BCD]:[ACE]=25:64$, and $[ABDE]=[ACE]-[BCD]=64-25=39$ in these units.

The required ratio is $\frac{39}{25}$.

**Answer: $\frac{39}{25}$**

hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-08.title: Formulas for the two numbers
hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-08.body:
The square in row $i$, column $j$ gets $10(i-1)+j$ from the first process and $10(j-1)+i$ from the second. Their sum is $11(i+j)-20$. Setting this equal to $101$: $11(i+j)=121$, so $i+j=11$.

With $1\le i,j\le10$ there are exactly $10$ such pairs: $(1,10),(2,9),\dots,(10,1)$.

**Answer: 10**

hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-10.title: Count line crossings
hmmt-feb-2004-gen1-10.body:
Walk along the needle from one end to the other. We enter a new triangle exactly when we cross a line of the tiling, so the number of triangles met is $1+$ (number of lines crossed).

The lines come in three directions, and parallel lines in a given direction are $\frac{\sqrt3}2$ apart. A needle of length $2$ cannot cross $4$ lines of one direction (that would need length more than $3\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\approx2.6$), so it crosses at most $3$ lines in each direction. Moreover it cannot cross $3$ lines in each of two directions: its endpoints would then have to lie in two opposite regions of the plane whose closest points are at distance $2$, and a needle of length $2$ (strictly less than the required distance, since the regions are open) cannot reach both.

So the crossings are at most $3+2+2=7$, giving at most $8$ triangles. This is attainable: a needle of length a little over $\sqrt3$ (so $<2$) placed suitably crosses $7$ lines, as in the standard picture.

**Answer: 8**
